Korean Companies Registering Trademarks in China: A Country Guide

K-beauty travels fast, and so do the people who file its names first. In China a Korean registration has no force of its own, and a Hangul name is not the sign Chinese consumers use. This guide sets out the filing rules from a Korean owner's point of view.

The Local-Agent Rule Applies Equally

A foreign applicant with no habitual residence or place of business in China must appoint a trademark agency lawfully established or registered in China. Article 11 of the 2026 Trademark Law continues the rule. For Korean companies, even those with heavy China sales, this is the starting constraint: the application is made by the local agent, not by head office.

A branch office in China does not by itself count as a place of business for this purpose, so the exemption does not apply. There is no special treatment for Korean applicants either, whatever cooperation exists between the Korean and Chinese IP authorities. MOIP, formerly KIPO, and CNIPA maintain contact on IP matters, but cooperation does not transfer a right or waive a filing requirement. Keep a standing power of attorney with your agent and keep the applicant name and address consistent across documents. More on the baseline in Who Can Register a Trademark in China.

Class Planning and the Chinese Name

A Korean brand name in Hangul is not the sign Chinese consumers use. An English word mark and a Chinese-character mark are separate rights in China. Register the official Chinese name, common transliterations and consumer-coined nicknames; similarity is judged by sound, form and meaning, so a phonetic lookalike can conflict even where the Latin marks differ.

Common K-beauty planningHow to treat it
Class 3, cosmeticsA common practical choice for the goods themselves
Class 35, retailOften considered for store and online retail services
Class 44, beauty servicesOften considered where salons or clinics are part of the model

This is portfolio planning, not a statutory requirement: the classes you need depend on the goods and services you actually offer, and the goods description must fit CNIPA's similar-group and sub-class practice. Plan with the class guide and clear the Chinese character forms before launch.

The Six-Month Priority Window and the Two Filing Routes

Under the Paris Convention, a mark first filed abroad may be filed in China within six months for the same mark and the same goods or services with a priority claim. The claim must be made in writing at the time of filing and a copy of the first application submitted within three months (Article 29 of the 2026 law, corresponding to old Article 25). First use at an international exhibition also gives a six-month priority right, a window easy to miss during distribution negotiations.

Two routes are available: a Madrid System registration designating China, examined by CNIPA under Chinese law with the goods description adapted to local sub-classes, or a direct national application. An international registration depends on the home basic registration for its first five years, the central-attack risk. For WIPO provisional refusals designating China, the response window is 15 days for ex officio refusals and 30 days for opposition-based refusals from receipt of the WIPO notification, with supplementary evidence within three months (WIPO official Time Limits table). Compare Madrid versus direct filing.

Documents, Language and Legalisation

Applications are filed in Chinese. Foreign-language entity certificates need a Chinese translation, and the applicant name and address must correspond in English and Chinese. Fix the official Chinese rendering once and reuse it; a mismatch with the corporate extract is a common avoidable objection.

A power of attorney is generally valid with a signature or seal, so do not assume notarisation or legalisation is always required. Where public documents do need authentication, the Hague Apostille Convention took effect for China on 7 November 2023: documents from contracting states use an Apostille instead of the traditional foreign-ministry-plus-embassy double legalisation, while non-contracting states still use consular legalisation. Applicability depends on the document type and what the receiving office currently accepts. Confirm current practice with the agent; never assume a fee or fixed timeline not in the official rules.

Squatting, Monitoring and the 2027 Law

Korean brands have faced lookalike stores and pre-emptive filings in China; the dispute case study collects reported examples. The controls are the same ones the 2027 law rewards. Effective 1 January 2027, Article 36 shortens the opposition period from three months to two months, which makes weekly watching necessary. Article 19 regulates bad-faith applications, and Article 57 lets CNIPA cancel a mark unused for three consecutive years on its own initiative, so archive dated use evidence.

Article 21 extends cross-class protection to unregistered well-known marks, Article 55 addresses licence recordal and statutory termination rights, and Article 46 introduces substantive examination of assignments. Platform and customs enforcement presuppose a Chinese registration certificate, so the filing is the gatekeeper. No official fees, success rates or special treatment for Korean applicants should be assumed; confirm the current official rules. Build the routine with the monitoring guide and the two-month watch SOP.

A distributor or OEM partner filing first is a recurring pattern. File before commercial discussions create a public trail, and keep the relationship documented.

Sources and Caveats

Sources: Trademark Law of the PRC (2026 Revision), Articles 11, 19, 21, 29, 36, 46, 55 and 57; the Paris Convention; the Hague Apostille Convention (in force for China from 7 November 2023); WIPO's official Time Limits table for provisional refusals; CNIPA practice on Chinese-language filings and class sub-groups. Class selections described above are common practice, not legal requirements. Procedures may be refined by implementing rules, so confirm current official requirements. This is general information, not legal advice.
